docs.title: JElib
docs.text:
JElib is a growing collection of Houdini tools designed to remove friction from your workflow, so you can stay focused on being creative.

At its core is the JE Asset Browser, an easy way to organize, browse, and access the assets you already have. Build your own reusable libraries of models, materials, setups, and other assets, then quickly find and bring them into your projects without digging through folders or rebuilding things you've already made. Support for Karma, Redshift & Octane.

The paid version currently includes additional tools for relinking external files and collecting project files.

docs.title: JE Asset Browser
docs.text:
Add any folder of assets — textures, materials, HDRIs, and geometry — and drag them into your scene. It works in both the OBJ and LOP (Solaris) contexts.

Install JElib, then point it at your assets.

docs.title: Other tools
docs.text:
• Collect Files — gather a scene's external assets into one place, ready to archive or hand off.
  • Relink Files — repath broken file references across your scene.

docs.title: Animation & sequences
docs.text: JElib handles three kinds of moving asset: frame sequences on disk, a single animated Alembic, and a rigged/animated FBX. Each is detected during the scan and imported as an animated setup — no manual $F wiring, no KineFX chain to build by hand.

docs.title: What gets detected
docs.text:
On disk Card badge Asset Info Numbered frame files — smoke_0001.vdb, anim.0001.abc, cache_v1.0001.bgeo.sc SEQ (a VDB sequence badges VDB) Frames row, e.g. 1-120 One .abc holding animation ABC — .fbx with a skin binding and animation curves ANIM — .fbx with a skin binding but no animation RIG —

Frame sequences collapse into one card with a $F template — the individual frames never clutter the grid. Two or more numbered files sharing a stem in the same folder make a family; LOD siblings (crate_lod0/1/2) are excluded, so they still group as LODs rather than a bogus 3-frame sequence.

Rigged FBX detection reads the file's own skin/animation markers, so it works on binary and ASCII FBX alike.

docs.title: Frame sequences
docs.text:
Supported for .abc, .bgeo / .bgeo.sc, .vdb, and .rs — see Supported file formats.

  • OBJ / SOP — the import reads the $F template, so the asset plays with the timeline as you scrub.
  • Solaris — the same, and the Bake .usd / Auto modes write a time-sampled USD over the sequence's frame range instead of freezing frame 1. A baked sequence cache is only rebuilt when its frames or range actually change.
  • VDB sequences drive the volume LOP's time-dependent sampling and get a volume shader for your renderer.
  • Missing frames are allowed but flagged in the import notes — the instancing retime below assumes a contiguous cache and copies pop where a frame is absent.
  • A $F sequence baked to USD authors no proxy or collision (simproxy) representation — those are static-asset-only. The render mesh bakes as usual.

$F sequences appear in Houdini's native Solaris Asset Catalog / Paint Instances gallery alongside rigged FBX (VDB and .rs proxy sequences don't — see Houdini's native galleries).

docs.title: Rigged & animated FBX
docs.text:
Drop one and JElib builds a KineFX character chain rather than a plain file SOP: fbxcharacterimport feeding a MotionClip pack → cycle → eval into a bonedeform, so the character actually deforms on the timeline. Rigged FBX default to import scale 1.0 (not the static-FBX 0.01).

In Solaris, the LOP Import combo swaps its two build modes for skeleton-aware ones:

Mode What you get USD Skel The live, editable graph in the stage — KineFX SOPs in a self-contained sopcreate host feeding a sopcharacterimport LOP Bake USD A real UsdSkel component on disk — SkelRoot / Skeleton / SkelAnimation, plus a proxy representation and the material under the component Use Cached USD References whatever cache exists; never re-bakes

Baked skeletons carry their materials, including textures from a Mixamo-style <name>.fbm sidecar folder that ordinary name-grouping can't associate.

Native frame placement

A clip bakes exactly where it sits in its own timeline — no loop, no normalize. USD holds the last sample past the end of the range, so the character freezes on its final pose rather than snapping back once the clip plays through. Looping is a separate, composition-time choice — see below.

docs.title: Loop
docs.text:
A Loop checkbox appears in the preview panel's Import Settings for any asset whose bake carries animation — a rigged/animated FBX or an $F sequence. VDB sequences and .rs proxy sequences don't get it; they don't bake through the same clip mechanism. Off (the default), the animation plays once and holds on its last frame; on, it repeats for the whole scene playback range.

Loop works in every Solaris import mode, live or baked, and for rigged FBX in the OBJ/SOP context too — JElib picks whichever mechanism the mode can actually carry:

Mode Mechanism Baked / referenced USD (Bake USD, Auto when it can write) A USD Value Clip wrapping the one-cycle cache, authored at drop time against the scene's playback range Rigged FBX, live (SOP Create, OBJ, USD Skel) The KineFX MotionClip cycle's Cycles After, sized to the playback range $F sequence, live (SOP Create, Component Builder) A seq_frame timeshift that wraps instead of clamping to the last frame

A $F sequence imported into an OBJ/SOP network is the one case Loop doesn't reach — that chain reads the frame straight off the scene, so it neither loops nor holds past the sequence's own range. Import it into Solaris to loop it.

You don't need to know which one applies — but the node it builds is a normal part of the network, so you can flip its loop toggle by hand afterwards if the scene's playback range changes.

Behaviour change: rigged FBX in live modes used to always loop

Earlier builds looped a rigged FBX's MotionClip unconditionally in SOP Create and OBJ. It now respects Loop like every other mode — plays once and holds unless you tick it.

docs.title: Per-instance time offset
docs.text:
With Create Instances on an animated asset, every copy would otherwise play in lockstep. The generated time-offset wrangle staggers them — a field of flowers that don't all bloom on the same frame.

The controls sit on that wrangle's parameters, next to the distribution and wind controls:

Parameter What it does Start Frame The sequence frame every copy starts on before its offset — raise it to skip preroll. Playback anchors to the scene's playback start, so the result reads the same on any timeline. Spread Mode Random (seeded per copy) · Step (ramped by copy index — a wave) · Attribute (frame driven directly by a point attribute) Spread Maximum frames of stagger across copies. 0 = lockstep. Loop Wrap the animation so copies stay spread across the whole range at every frame. Off: each copy plays once and holds on its last frame. Seed Random mode only. Offset Remap Step mode only — reshapes the linear index ramp that scales the offset. Offset Attribute Attribute mode only — the 0–1 point attribute to scale the offset by (default factor). A missing attribute reads as 0, i.e. same timing for every copy.

How each source is retimed — JElib picks the mechanism the format can actually sustain:

Source Mechanism Notes Single animated .abc Per-copy Alembic time on packed prims The viewport can't draw per-copy Alembic time — it renders correctly. An archive whose content doesn't actually move is treated as static, even if it carries a time range .bgeo / .bgeo.sc sequence Bare points, each loading its own frame file Karma and Redshift honour the per-point material; Octane uses the object material .rs proxy sequence Same, via the proxy file per point Redshift only .abc sequence — Create Instances is unavailable. Every offset copy needs its own archive open, which is unusably slow. Bake to .bgeo.sc and instance that instead. Solaris / USD A Cache LOP + Retime Instances, with bucketed per-instance offsets Automatic — no separate offset controls in the preview panel. Scattered copies each play the animation at their own phase, on a native USD PointInstancer. See Per-instance time offset in the stage.

Both halves are on the same wrangle

Whichever mechanism is used, the parameters above are identical — you dial Spread Mode / Spread / Seed the same way for a .abc prop and a .bgeo.sc cache.

docs.title: Add your libraries
docs.text:
On first launch, JElib asks where your assets are — pick your assets folder (local drive, external drive, NAS, Dropbox / OneDrive / Google Drive / iCloud) and it adds the libraries it finds inside.

JElib stores one base folder per machine ($JELIB_ASSETS) and writes your library paths relative to it ($JELIB_ASSETS/StudioLibrary, …). That keeps a single config portable across your own machines: each machine points $JELIB_ASSETS at wherever its copy lives, and every library resolves.

Add libraries from anywhere else — any path — in the Libraries tab. Re-open the first-run setup any time from Libraries → Re-run setup….

docs.title: Scene-local assets ($HIP/tex)
docs.text:
Working on a shot or project where textures live right next to the scene file? Tick Show $HIP/tex in the Libraries tab footer.

Whenever a tex folder exists beside your saved .hip file, JElib automatically surfaces a Local Library at the very top of the navigation tree. It follows your active scene dynamically as you open or save scenes, scans its contents fresh, and wires imported textures with portable $HIP/tex/… paths so your project travels cleanly to any machine without relinking.

See Libraries tab reference for details.

Multi-machine & remote storage

Cloud/NAS libraries, on-demand caching, and using one config across several machines have their own guide — see Remote & cloud libraries.

docs.title: Texture atlases
docs.text: A texture atlas is a packed sheet holding many pieces on one image — foliage leaf cards, decals, ground debris, trim pieces. Import one and JElib doesn't just slap it on a flat plane: it traces the packed pieces off the sheet onto a carrier as separate cards, ready to scatter.

docs.title: Importing an atlas
docs.text:
Atlas assets from Quixel and Fab are detected automatically. Drop one in and JElib routes it through the Atlas Splitter — it reads the atlas's opacity and colour maps and traces each packed piece into its own card on a generated carrier, instead of a single flat quad.

Have a loose texture you know is an atlas? Select it and tick Import as Atlas in the preview panel:

Load this texture through the atlas splitter HDA (separates packed leaf cards / decals onto a carrier) instead of as a flat texture.

It's an explicit opt-in (off by default), shown for loose textures.

Needs the Atlas Splitter HDA

Splitting relies on the JE_Atlas_Splitter HDA. If it isn't installed, the atlas loads onto a plain flat grid with no piece splitting — and if you asked for instances, JElib warns you that the whole grid will be copied.

docs.title: Scatter the cards
docs.text:
Atlases shine with instancing: each traced piece becomes a variant, so turning on Create Instances scatters the cards across your points with per-card scale, rotation, and tilt.

Set Source Up to +Z for cards

Card geometry usually faces +Z (the card normal), but the instancing Source Up control defaults to +Y (upright models/plants). Switch it to +Z so scattered cards orient correctly. Turn off the "long axis → X" rotation for non-foliage atlases like decals or pebbles.

docs.title: Typical uses
docs.text: Foliage leaf cards for trees and bushes, scattered decals and ground debris, trim and pebble sheets — anything shipped as many small pieces packed into one texture.

docs.title: Find & organize
docs.text: However big your library gets, four tools get you to the right asset fast: browse, search, filter, and favorites.

docs.title: Browse your folders
docs.text:
By default the grid shows every asset under the folder you've selected in the left-hand tree — sub-folders flattened into one view. That's great for scanning, less so for big trees.

Turn on Browse in the toolbar to walk the tree like Finder instead: the grid shows only this folder's contents — sub-folders appear as tiles alongside the assets that live at this level.

  • Double-click a folder tile to enter it.
  • Double-click the .. tile at the top of the grid to go up one level. (It's hidden once you're at a library root.)
  • From the keyboard: Enter on a folder tile enters it, Backspace goes up one level, and the arrow keys move between tiles.
  • The left tree stays in sync — select a folder there, or drill in the grid; either drives the other.

Browse off = search everything

Leave Browse off when you want search and filters to sweep the whole library at once. Turn it on when you know roughly where the asset lives and want to click your way there.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
Type in the Search assets… field in the toolbar. It filters live as you type, matching asset names and tags in the current view.

  1. Select a folder or library in the navigation tree.
  2. Type a name or tag into Search assets….
  3. Select a result to inspect it before loading it into your scene.

To search by tag, use the tag: keyword — everything before it is a name query, everything after is a comma-separated tag list:

You type You get concrete assets named concrete tag: gravel assets tagged gravel concrete tag: road, urban concrete assets tagged road or urban

The tag: keyword highlights as you type, and known tags auto-complete.

Two search fields

The leftmost field jumps you to a collection (a saved location); the Search assets… field filters the assets in view. This page is about the second one.

docs.title: Filter
docs.text:
Click Filter in the toolbar to open the filter panel. Toggles apply live; the button stays lit while any filter is active.

  1. Click Filter.
  2. Choose the asset type, format, renderer, tag, or range you need.

The toolbar reports the number of active filters and shows a removable chip above the grid, so it is always clear why the current results are narrowed.

  • Favorites — show only starred assets.
  • Asset Type — Material, HDRI, Model, Plant, Atlas, Texture, Node Tree.
  • Format — narrow models to one geometry format: FBX, OBJ, ABC, USD, BGEO.
  • User Saved Materials — your own saved materials by renderer (Redshift, Octane, Karma) or USD Materials.
  • Tags — one toggle per tag present in the library.
  • Filter Range — flip All Libraries to widen search and filters to every library instead of just the current view. Clear resets everything.

Active filters also show as chips above the grid — click a chip to drop it, or Clear all to reset.

docs.title: Favorites
docs.text:
Star the assets you reach for often and pull them up in one click.

  • Hover a tile and click the star at the top-left of its thumbnail. Favorited assets keep the star showing.
  • Right-click one or more selected assets → Add to Favorites / Remove from Favorites (the label counts your selection).

To see them, toggle the star button in the toolbar (or Favorites in the filter panel) — favorites are shown within your current view, so combine them with Browse or All Libraries to scope wide or narrow. Favorites persist across sessions.

docs.title: Supported file formats
docs.text: What JElib recognizes when it scans a library or receives a file — and what happens when you import each kind.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
Extension What it is OBJ / SOP Solaris (LOP) Sequences .fbx Mesh, LODs, multi-piece kits — and rigged/animated characters file SOP (or split per piece); a KineFX chain when rigged Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD — USD Skel · Bake USD when rigged — .obj Mesh file SOP Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD — .abc Alembic — preserves the source hierarchy and per-piece names Dedicated alembic SOP Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD Yes — $F frame families .bgeo / .bgeo.sc Houdini geometry file SOP Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD Yes — $F frame families .gltf / .glb glTF mesh (Sketchfab and similar downloads ship this) Dedicated import chain, LOD-aware Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD — .usd / .usdc / .usda / .usdz Already USD Referenced directly — no baking Referenced directly — no baking — .vdb OpenVDB volume file SOP + a volume shader for your renderer Native volume LOP Yes — $F frame families .rs Redshift Proxy redshift_packedProxySOP Native RS_Proxy LOP Yes — $F frame families

See Working in Solaris for what each LOP Import mode does, and Preferences → USD to set your default. Anything animated — a $F sequence, an animated Alembic, a rigged FBX — is covered on Animation & sequences.

VDB and RS Proxy carry their own shading

Both formats skip the generic material-building path. A VDB gets a dedicated volume shader per renderer (Redshift/Octane/Karma); an RS Proxy carries its baked-in shading from export, so Create Material isn't offered for either — there's nothing for JElib to build.

Same stem, several formats

Crate.fbx next to Crate.obj gives you one card per format — the first format present keeps the bare name, the rest are suffixed (Crate (OBJ)). They share one thumbnail, and the Format filter narrows the grid to a single one.

RS Proxy is Redshift-only

.rs files render only in Redshift — Octane and Karma have no equivalent proxy format. Import still works with another renderer selected; you just won't get a shaded result until you switch to Redshift.

docs.title: Textures & PBR maps
docs.text: .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .tif, .tiff, .tx, .tga.

docs.title: HDRIs
docs.text: .hdr, .hdri, and .exr — an .exr is only treated as an HDRI when its filename signals it (hdri, env, panorama, latlong, equirect, ibl, …); otherwise it's read as a texture/render pass, since most .exr files aren't environment maps.

docs.title: Color palettes
docs.text: .ase, .gpl, .aco, .swatches, and a .txt whose name or contents look like a swatch list. See Color palettes.

docs.title: Node trees & saved materials
docs.text: Materials and node networks you save from Houdini live as .json inside the browser's own library folders — see Save to the browser. They aren't something you'd drop in from outside Houdini.

docs.title: Import into your scene
docs.text: Dragging an asset in is the core move — JElib builds the nodes and wires the material for your renderer. If you just want the quick version, see Import your first asset. This page covers every way to import and every option along the way.

docs.title: Three ways to import
docs.text:
• Drag a tile from the grid into the network editor or the viewport.
  • Double-click a tile, or select it and press Enter (loads every selected tile).
  • Select a tile and click Load into Scene in the preview panel.

You can drag a multi-selection too — Ctrl/Shift-click several tiles, then drag them in together.

Viewport drops place at the drop point

Drop a model or plant on the 3D viewport and it lands where you released it — on the geometry surface under the cursor, else the ground plane, else the origin. This works in both the OBJ and Solaris (LOP-stage) contexts. A multi-drop fans the assets out side by side, and HDRIs become the active renderer's dome light. This applies to drags from the browser; OS file drops on the viewport keep Houdini's own behavior.

Drop a material onto an object to assign it

Drag a material tile onto geometry in the viewport and JElib builds it for your active renderer and assigns it to whatever is under the cursor — including bare primitive shapes and, in Solaris, USD prims. It targets the part under the cursor (a material slot / named part, or a GeomSubset in Solaris) and falls back to the whole object — hold Ctrl to flip that for one drop. The whole drag-and-drop is a single undo step.

docs.title: Drag files in from outside Houdini
docs.text:
You don't have to go through the browser at all. Drag a texture, PBR set, HDRI, or model straight from your OS file manager (Explorer/Finder) onto the network editor, and JElib imports it exactly like a browser drop — same nodes, same material for your active renderer, honouring your import settings (Force Absolute File Paths, Prefer 16-bit, Material Only…).

  • Drop a folder and JElib reads it as one asset: geometry + a PBR set becomes a model with its material built together; a textures-only folder becomes one material. LOD siblings (crate_lod0/1/2.fbx) collapse into a single model at your Default LOD (Preferences → Import); a folder holding only a _High source mesh imports that. Drop a single hand-picked file and it imports just that.
  • This is controlled by Handle External File Drops (Preferences → Import → Advanced, on by default). Turn it off to hand OS drops back to Houdini or other tools.

What's covered

External drops work over the network editor while the panel is open — not the viewport, not parameter fields, and not while the panel is closed or hidden behind another tab. Recognized files (textures/HDRIs/models) are claimed; anything else passes straight through to Houdini.

It follows your context

Drop into a LOP/Solaris network and JElib builds USD; drop into OBJ and it builds SOP-based geo and a matnet. With Import Into Active Network on (Preferences → Import → Advanced), it imports where you already are.

docs.title: Pick your renderer first
docs.text:
The renderer selector in the toolbar — Karma · Redshift · Octane — decides which material JElib builds. Your choice is remembered, so it's always your engine on launch.

Local Library imports are portable

Importing from the Local Library ($HIP/tex) writes $HIP/tex/… texture paths, so the hip and its textures travel to another machine or artist without relinking.

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text: Asset What JElib builds Model / geometry a geo object with a file/Alembic SOP chain PBR texture set / material a material network for your renderer HDRI a dome light Color palette a ramp or gradient node — you pick the form (Color palettes) Saved material / node tree the saved shader, rebuilt for its renderer USD model a reference (or sublayer) into the stage

docs.title: Replace an existing material
docs.text:
Select one or more material containers in the network editor and import a material with Shift held (Shift-drop, or Shift+Load): instead of adding a sibling, JElib rebuilds the selected material in place — same spot in the network, named after the new material — and repoints existing assignments so your objects keep their material. Without Shift, imports always create a new material and leave your selection alone.

Shift-dropping several assets onto several selected materials replaces them pairwise, in the order you read the network (top-to-bottom, left-to- right). Extra assets import as new; extra selected materials are left untouched.

Diving inside a material container works without Shift — importing there always rebuilds that material in place.

docs.title: Import options (preview panel)
docs.text:
Select an asset and the preview panel's Import Settings let you change how this one import behaves — overriding your Preferences defaults without touching them:

First select the model card. The controls then appear in that asset's Import Settings panel at the right of the Browser:

  1. Turn on Create Instances to build a ready-to-edit scatter setup.
  2. Choose the instance method (Copy to Points or Scatter Instances).

  3. Click Load into Scene.

  4. Material Only — build just the shader, no geometry. Great for reusing a texture set on your own geo.

  5. Create Instances — scatter the asset as instances, with VEX distribution and wind controls (model/plant/atlas). See Instance a model, plant, or atlas.
  6. Instance method (next to Create Instances) — Copy to Points (default) or Scatter Instances (H22). Both this and the Create Instances toggle stay where you set them as you click through cards.
  7. Loop (rigged/animated FBX and $F sequences only) — repeat the animation for the whole scene range instead of holding on the last frame. See Animation & sequences.
  8. Create Material — make a blank material network even when no textures were detected.
  9. Import as Atlas — route a packed texture through the Atlas Splitter so decals and leaf cards land on a carrier instead of a flat plane.
  10. LOD — pick a level of detail when the asset ships several.
  11. UV Mode / Resolution — projection and texture resolution for the material.
  12. LOP Import (in Solaris) — how non-USD geo enters the stage: USD Auto Import, SOP Create, Component Builder, Build USD, or Use Cached USD. Defaults live in Preferences → USD.

Full control-by-control detail is on the Browse tab reference.

docs.title: Instance a model, plant, or atlas
docs.text:
Turn on Create Instances (offered for models, plants, and atlases) and JElib does more than import the asset — it builds a scatter setup that auto-distributes the asset as instances, with VEX controls to shape the spread and even add wind.

Copies are packed primitives, so scattering thousands stays light. The asset is wired in as the prototype on its own input, kept separate from the scatter points.

Start on a demo grid, then repoint it

Out of the box it scatters onto a demo grid — a starting point, not scene-aware. Wire your own geometry into the WIRE_USER_POINTS_HERE object merge and flip the switch_points_source switch to distribute across real points instead.

Distribution controls live as parameters on the generated wrangle nodes:

  • Variant / Piece — which piece each instance gets (Random or Step). Atlas cards, plant variants, and multi-mesh pieces each become a selectable variant.
  • Pscale — random per-instance scale (size min/max, exponent, seed).
  • Rotation — up-axis, cone angle, random rotation range, snap-to-90°, seeds.

Motion / wind — a wind control adds animated sway, off by default. Dial Directional Amplitude + Wind Direction for a steady lean, or Evolution Amplitude with Frequency and Speed for noise-driven motion.

Time offset — when the asset is itself animated (a $F sequence or an animated Alembic), a time-offset wrangle staggers the copies so they don't play in lockstep: Start Frame, Spread Mode (Random / Step / Attribute), Spread, Loop, Seed. Full detail on Animation & sequences.

Atlas & plant specifics

Atlas cards each become a variant — this needs the Atlas Splitter HDA installed (without it, the whole grid is copied and JElib warns you). A plain single-mesh model with no variant attributes scatters as a single prototype. In Solaris, instancing builds a native USD PointInstancer instead.

docs.title: Where materials are built
docs.text: By default JElib builds the material in whatever network you're viewing (Current Network) — a per-asset matnet at the cursor, or straight into a matnet/vopnet you're already in. Switch to a fixed home — the geo network (SOP Context), a shared /mat (Global), or a shared /obj/matnet (OBJ Context) — in Preferences → Import → Material Network — see Preferences.

docs.title: Import your first asset
docs.text:
With a library set up, getting an asset into your scene is a single drag. JElib builds the nodes and creates the material for you — no file SOP, no manual shader setup.

First, set up a library

If the Browse grid is empty, point JElib at your assets first — see Add your libraries.

docs.title: 1. Choose your renderer
docs.text:
At the top of the panel, the renderer selector — Karma · Redshift · Octane — decides which material JElib builds when you import. Pick yours before you drag.

Tip

Your choice is remembered across sessions — pick once and it's always your engine on launch.

docs.title: 2. Drag an asset into your scene
docs.text:
From the Browse grid, drag any asset tile into Houdini's network editor (or the viewport). JElib catches the drop and builds the right nodes in place.

Two other ways to do the same thing:

  • Double-click a tile, or select it and press Enter.
  • Select it, then click Load into Scene in the preview panel.

docs.title: 3. What you get
docs.text:
JElib creates the nodes the asset needs, for the renderer you chose:

Asset What's created Model / geometry a geo object with a file or Alembic SOP Material / texture a material network for your renderer (materiallibrary in Solaris/LOPs, matnet in /mat) HDRI a dome light Color palette a ramp material

JElib creates the material for your active renderer — assign it and render.

Just the material?

Tick Material Only in the preview panel before loading to build the shader without any geometry.

Next: Import into your scene — every asset type JElib understands and every option along the way, from Material Only to texture atlases.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Requires Houdini 20.5, 21.x, or 22.x

JElib runs on the Python these ship (3.11 on 20.5/21.x, 3.13 on 22.x). On older Houdini builds the panel and menu simply won't appear.

  1. Unzip the JElib folder anywhere — the installer copies it to a stable location for you.
  2. Run the installer:
    • Windows — double-click Install_JElib_Windows.bat. If SmartScreen warns, click More info → Run anyway.
    • macOS — double-click Install_JElib_macOS.command. The first time, macOS may say "unidentified developer": right-click → Open → Open.
    • Any OS fallback — run it with Houdini's Python: "<Houdini>/bin/hython" setup_jelib.py
  3. Answer the prompts (mostly just press Enter). The installer detects your Houdini version, copies the code to ~/Documents/JElib, and writes the package config into Houdini's packages folder.
  4. Restart Houdini, then open JElib → Asset Browser.
  5. On first launch, JElib asks where your assets are — see Add your libraries.

Manual install (no installer)

Copy JElib.json from the unzipped folder into Houdini's packages/ directory (e.g. ~/Documents/houdini21.0/packages/ on Windows, ~/Library/Preferences/houdini/21.0/packages/ on macOS), set its JELIB value (EDIT_ME) to the full path of your unzipped JElib folder, then restart Houdini.

docs.title: Color palettes
docs.text: A color palette is a swatch file — the kind you export from Photoshop, Procreate, Coolors, or a brand style guide. JElib reads it, shows it as a swatch grid in the browser. You can then import the colors as regular Color SOPs or as ramps (VEX, Karma, Redshift, Octane).

docs.title: Adding palettes
docs.text:
Drop swatch files into any folder JElib scans and they show up, badged PAL with a swatch-grid thumbnail.

Supported files:

Format Extension Adobe Swatch Exchange .ase GIMP palette .gpl Photoshop swatches .aco Procreate swatches .swatches Plain hex list .txt (only if the name contains palette, colors, swatch, pantone, hex…)

Adding a file to a scanned folder is all it takes — or save one straight from the scene, see Saving a palette below.

RGB swatches only

JElib reads RGB colors from .ase/.aco files; swatches authored in CMYK, LAB, or grayscale are skipped.

docs.title: Importing a palette
docs.text:
A palette isn't a finished material — it's a building block. Drag one in (or Load into Scene) and JElib asks how you want it, via the Load Palette dialog — one of five outputs:

Output What you get Color SOP (one node per color) a color SOP per swatch — good for assigning flat colors to geo VEX Ramp (default) an attribwrangle with a color ramp driving @Cd Redshift Ramp an RSRamp gradient node Karma Ramp a kma_rampconst gradient node Octane Ramp an octane gradient node

The three renderer ramps are created inside a matnet named color_palette, ready to plug into a shader as a color source. You can build any of them whatever your active renderer is — the choice decides the node, not the scene.

Apply straight to a ramp you already have

Select a single supported ramp node first — an RSRamp, Karma ramp, Octane gradient, a Color SOP in Ramp from Attribute mode, or an attribwrangle with a color ramp — then load the palette. JElib skips the dialog and writes the colors straight into that node.

Inside a material builder (a Redshift or Octane vopnet, a USD material builder, or a MaterialX subnet in a Material Library) there's no dialog either: JElib creates that renderer's ramp right there in the builder.

docs.title: How the colors map
docs.text:
Each swatch becomes one ramp key, in file order, evenly spaced across the ramp with linear interpolation — so you get a smooth gradient between colors, not hard bands. There's no limit on the number of colors.

Colors are converted to ACEScg for the Color SOP, VEX, Redshift, and Karma outputs; the Octane output uses linear sRGB.

The preview panel shows a Colors: N count for a selected palette. The material and geometry import toggles (Material Only, LOD, and so on) don't apply to palettes.

docs.title: Saving a palette
docs.text:
Palettes go the other way too. Select ramp nodes or Color SOPs and save them like any other node setup — right-click → Save Asset [JE], or drag them onto a folder in the nav tree or onto the grid (see Save to the browser). When every selected node is a Color SOP or a supported ramp — an RSRamp, Karma ramp, Octane gradient, or an attribwrangle with a color ramp — JElib writes an .ase swatch file instead of a node asset. It appears as a palette card right away, loads into any of the five outputs, and opens in Photoshop or Illustrator.

  • A ramp becomes one swatch per key, in ramp order, named <node>_01, <node>_02, … Key positions aren't kept — a palette is an ordered list, and loading it back spaces the colors evenly.
  • A Color SOP set to Constant becomes one swatch, named after the node; set to Ramp from Attribute its ramp is saved like any other ramp. The other Color Types have no color of their own, so a selection containing one is saved as a node asset instead.
  • A key hidden under another key at the very start or end of a ramp (an RSRamp's default black and white, say, with your own keys dragged on top) isn't part of the gradient you see, so it isn't saved either.
  • Colors are converted back from ACEScg to sRGB (Octane gradients from linear sRGB), the reverse of loading. A swatch file is 8-bit sRGB, so a color outside the sRGB gamut is clipped on the way out.

Mix in anything else — a box, a subnet, a shader — and the selection is saved as a regular node asset instead. Nothing asks; the nodes decide.

docs.title: Parameter menus
docs.text: JElib adds two items to the right-click menu of any string parameter in Houdini — handy for jumping to files and keeping paths portable. Right-click any file/path parameter to access them directly at the top of the menu:

docs.title: Open Folder [JE]
docs.text: Reveals the parameter's file in Explorer/Finder. It expands the value first, so $VAR, $F, and <UDIM> tokens resolve to the real location — you land in the actual folder without decoding the expression by hand. If the expanded path is a file it's selected; otherwise its containing folder opens.

docs.title: Convert to Relative/Absolute Path [JE]
docs.text:
One click flips the path between a portable $VAR-relative form (e.g. $ASSETS/wood/oak.exr) and a concrete absolute path — whichever applies. It recognises the studio roots $JOB, $ASSETS, $HIP, $STUDIO, and the vendor library roots, and picks the most specific match. Frame and UDIM tokens are left intact.

Select several string parameters and it converts them all at once.

Why it matters

Relative paths survive moving the project or handing the file to another machine or artist; absolute paths are handy for debugging or pasting elsewhere. This is the same portability idea as Use Relative Path on libraries, applied to any parameter.

docs.title: Browse tab
docs.text:
The Browse tab is the main workspace: a toolbar, the asset grid, a preview panel, and the navigation tree. It has two ways to navigate a library:

  • Grid view shows the assets in the current folder, ready to browse, search, select, and load.
  • Browse view shows the current folder's subfolders first. Open a folder tile to drill down; use Backspace to go back up.
Grid viewBrowse and select assets. Browse viewDrill into library folders.

For the how do I browse/search/filter/favorite workflow, see Find & organize — this page covers everything else on the tab.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
Left to right:

Control What it does Collection field Search and jump to a saved collection. Type to autocomplete; the dropdown arrow lists all collections. Search · Filter · Favorites Covered in Find & organize. Browse Toggle Finder-style drill-down. See Find & organize. Maps Show individual texture maps instead of grouped sets. View Switch between grid and list view. Thumbnail size Slider, 64–512 px. Double-click to reset. Renderer Active renderer for material and texture imports. Your pick is remembered across sessions — this selector is the setting. Reload Reload libraries. Shift-click to force-rescan all. A plain click fully re-checks every NAS library by default (that's the accurate-but-slower option) — turn on a library's Trust Cache on Reload (nav tree, right-click) to make a plain click skip that check for it. Cloud-backed libraries with Trust Cloud Library Cache enabled behave the same way. See Remote & synced libraries.

When any filter is active, a chip row appears below the toolbar with a Clear all link.

docs.title: The asset grid
docs.text:
Each tile shows a thumbnail, the asset name (elided if long), and a type badge (EXR, FBX, VDB, RS, UDIM, SEQ, ANIM / RIG for a rigged FBX, a category, or a renderer name for saved materials). Overlays: a renderer logo (bottom-left, plus a usd logo for USD-backed assets), the favorite star, and a small dot showing cloud/sync state (hover the dot for a plain-language explanation).

Interaction

  • Click a tile to load it into the preview panel.
  • Double-click an asset to load it into the scene; double-click a folder tile to enter it.
  • Ctrl / Shift-click to multi-select.
  • Keyboard — arrow keys, Home/End and Page Up/Down move the selection (the preview follows); Enter loads the selected asset(s) or enters a folder tile; Backspace goes up one folder in Browse mode.
  • Drag tiles out of the grid to drop them into your scene.

docs.title: Right-click an asset
docs.text:
Item Action New Directory… / New Sub-Directory… Make a folder (with …and Move N Assets… variants in your own libraries). Open Source Folder Reveal the asset in Explorer/Finder. Copy Path / Copy Relative Path Copy the file path. Delete Asset… Delete the asset (writable libraries only). Make Available Offline / Make Online-only Cache or un-cache the asset locally (on-demand libraries). Generate Thumbnail Render a thumbnail for the asset. Open Thumbnail Folder / Delete Thumbnail Manage its cached thumbnail. Delete USD Cache Remove the baked .usd sidecar.

Right-clicking a folder tile instead offers Open Folder, New / Rename / Delete Directory… (in writable libraries).

docs.title: Preview panel
docs.text:
Selecting an asset fills the preview panel on the right:

  • Thumbnail and name at the top.
  • Asset Info — type · format · size, local-cache status, per-type details (colors, nodes, channels, UDIM tiles, frames…), and clickable tag pills (click a tag to search it).
  • USD — cache state and prim/variant/material info, when relevant.

  • Import Settings — per-asset options shown only when they apply: LOD, LOP Import mode, Resolution, UV Mode, the instance method (Copy to Points / Scatter Instances (H22)), Loop (any asset baking to animated USD — rigged/animated FBX or an $F sequence), and toggles for Create Instances, Material Only, Create Material, and Import as Atlas.

    Create Instances and the instance method are sticky — the choice carries to the next card you click. Create Instances is unavailable (and says why) on an .abc frame sequence; see Animation & sequences.

The primary Load into Scene button (bottom) imports the asset with those settings. With Material Only ticked it loads just the shader, no geometry.

Per-asset overrides

Import Settings here override the Preferences defaults for this one asset — handy for pulling a lower LOD or a material-only copy without changing your global settings.

docs.title: Navigation tree
docs.text:
The left tree mirrors your libraries and their folders. Names show uppercased, with optional asset counts (toggle in Preferences). A Favorites node appears at the top whenever you have favorites, and a Local Library node pins near the top when Show $HIP/tex is on and a tex folder sits next to the current scene file.

Right-click a folder for:

Item Action Open Folder · Copy Path Reveal or copy the folder. New / Rename / Delete Directory… Manage folders (writable libraries). Reload This Library Rescan just this library — always checks the source fully, even when Trust Cache on Reload is on. Trust Cache on Reload (NAS libraries only) Skip re-checking this library on a plain Reload — see Remote & synced libraries. Make Available Offline Cache the whole folder (on-demand libraries). Disable on This Machine Turn the library off locally. Scan on This Machine (any folder or collection below the root) Uncheck to stop scanning it here — it stays in the tree as a dimmed (not scanned) entry; right-click it again to re-include it. Works on vendor collections too (a single Greyscalegorilla material pack), where JElib skips that pack's folders by their shared name prefix. Per machine, so a NAS-bound laptop can skip an unused vendor subfolder (a Greyscalegorilla hdris, say) while a workstation keeps it. Not offered where a collection's folders can't be told apart from its neighbours' (some Quixel categories). Hide the dimmed entries with Show Unscanned Folders in Preferences. Remove from Browser Drop the library from the list (files untouched).

docs.title: Libraries tab
docs.text:
The Libraries tab is where you add, remove, and manage the folders JElib scans for assets. Each row is one library.

For the concepts behind base folders and portable paths, see Add your libraries. This page is the control-by-control reference.

docs.title: The library table
docs.text:
Libraries are listed in a three-column table:

Column Shows Name the library's display name (double-click to rename) Path its folder (double-click to edit; hover for the full path) Status scan result — see below

Drag a row to reorder it, or use the ↑ / ↓ buttons in the footer (Move library up / Move library down). Order here is the order libraries appear in the nav tree.

Ctrl- or Shift-click selects multiple rows — the right-click actions (Disable / Enable on This Machine, Remove) then apply to the whole selection at once.

docs.title: What Status means
docs.text:
Status Meaning 1,234 assets found (the count) 0 folder exists but is empty … still scanning Cloud a cloud folder that's paused or still syncing Not found the folder is missing No path no path set yet Disabled turned off on this machine

Hover the count on a NAS library with Trust Cache on Reload turned on (Remote & synced libraries) for a reminder that a plain Reload won't check that library for changes.

docs.title: Add a library
docs.text:
Three ways:

  • Click Add… in the footer and pick a folder (Select Library Folder).
  • Drag a folder from Explorer/Finder straight onto the table.
  • Right-click empty space in the table → Add Library…

The new library is named after the folder and starts editable and writable.

docs.title: Remove a library
docs.text: Select a row and click Remove, or right-click the row → Remove Library (with several rows selected: Remove N Libraries — one undo step). There's no confirmation — but it's undoable (Ctrl+Z). Removing a library only drops it from the list; it never touches the files on disk.

docs.title: The Selected Library inspector
docs.text:
Select a row to open the Selected Library pane on the right (drag the divider to collapse it). It exposes everything about that one library:

Path

  • The folder path, with a chooser button (Select Library Folder).
  • Use Relative Path rewrites the path as $JELIB_ASSETS/… so your config stays portable across machines (toggles to Use Absolute Path). See Add your libraries.
  • The / button flips between forward slashes and backslashes.

Toggles

  • Read-Only Library — treat the library as managed by an external tool. Disables folder drag-move, new folder, delete, and drops. Auto-set for Greyscalegorilla / Quixel / Fab on first run.
  • Enabled on This Machine — turn the library on or off for this computer only. Saved locally; your synced library list is unchanged.
  • Expand in Nav Tree — start this library expanded (uncheck to start collapsed).
  • Enable On-Demand Caching — copy assets locally on demand from a remote root. When on, set the Remote Source Root below.

Remote Source Root (when caching is on) — the remote/cloud path assets are pulled from.

Local cache size (when caching is on) — Measure reports exactly what the library's local cache holds on disk (size and file count). Evict Library… frees that space by deleting only files verified to still exist on the remote — anything not mirrored survives, the remote is never touched, and files re-download on next use. See Remote & cloud libraries.

Ignore Pattern / Ignore Directories — chips that exclude matching files or folders from scanning.

Notes — free text; saves itself a moment after you stop typing.

Read-only vendor libraries

Greyscalegorilla, Quixel, and Fab libraries are flagged Read-Only automatically — JElib never writes into those trees. On-demand caching still works for them, because it only reads the remote and writes to your local cache.

docs.title: Re-run setup
docs.text: Re-run setup… (footer) reopens the first-run welcome flow to re-detect your assets folder and add any libraries it finds. It's additive — it never removes or rewrites libraries you already have.

docs.title: Show $HIP/tex (Local Library)
docs.text:
The Show $HIP/tex checkbox (footer) surfaces a Local Library at the top of the nav tree whenever a tex folder sits next to the current scene file. It follows the scene — opening, Save As, or a new scene re-resolves it — and it simply isn't listed when no tex folder exists (it never appears in the library table).

Imports from it write portable $HIP/tex/… texture paths, so the hip and its textures travel to another machine or artist without relinking. Textures dropped into the folder appear on any Reload — this library is always scanned fresh.

docs.title: Startup collection
docs.text:
The Startup dropdown (footer, right) picks a collection to auto-select the next time the panel opens. It's filled from your nav tree after each scan.

No manual rescan needed

There's no Scan button here — editing a path, adding or removing a library, or toggling Enabled rescans automatically. The Status column always reflects the latest scan.

docs.title: Preferences tab
docs.text:
Every setting on the Preferences tab applies live — there's no Save or Apply button, and nothing needs a restart. Settings are grouped top to bottom as below.

Reset a single setting

Ctrl+Middle-click any control to reset just that one to its default. The Reset to Defaults button (bottom right) resets them all — library paths are never touched.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: Setting What it does Theme Visual theme. Default inherits Houdini's look — on Houdini 22 it follows your live color theme (Edit ▸ Color Theme), accent and all, updating as you edit it. Minimal, Neutral (hueless greys — thumbnails are the only colour), and XSI (Softimage-inspired) are bundled skins. Drop more <name>.json files in the plugin's themes/ folder to add your own. Keep Window Above Other Apps When the browser floats in its own window, keep it above every other application's windows — not just Houdini's. No effect while docked in a pane. Saved per machine; the default matches your platform's native behavior (on for macOS, off for Windows).

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
How assets come into your scene.

Setting Options Default Material Network Current Network (build where you're viewing — a per-asset matnet at the cursor, or directly inside a matnet/vopnet; /mat in a non-material context) · Global (shared /mat) · OBJ Context (a shared /obj/matnet) · SOP Context (per-asset matnet inside the geo network) Current Network Material Assignment shop_materialpath (explicit per-prim path) · Name Attribute (group by name string) shop_materialpath Material Type Standard Material · Open PBR Material Standard Material Bump Map Mode Normal Map · Bump Map · Displacement Normal Map (bump falls back when no normal exists) Default Projection UV · Triplanar (per-material override lives in the preview panel) UV Default LOD LOD 0 (highest detail) · Lowest Detail · High / Source Mesh LOD 0

The renderer has no preference: the toolbar selector is remembered across sessions, so your last choice is your engine on every launch.

Default LOD is where a multi-LOD asset starts: the inspector's LOD picker and folder drops from Explorer/Finder both default here. High / Source Mesh applies when the asset ships an unreduced source (e.g. Quixel High) and falls back to LOD 0 otherwise.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
Collapsed by default; click Advanced to expand.

Setting What it does Default Import Into Active Network Import inside the network you're already in, if it's compatible; otherwise create a new container at the top level. On Default Create Instances Default state for the per-asset Create Instances toggle — auto-adds a scatter chain to atlas/model/plant drops. Off Relative Material Node Path Store shop_materialpath as a relative node path (../matnet/shader) instead of absolute. On Force Absolute File Paths Write absolute OS paths into the scene instead of $VAR/… tokens. Off Handle External File Drops Import textures, PBR sets, HDRIs, and models dragged from your OS file manager onto the network editor (while this panel is open). Off hands those drops back to Houdini. On Show Asset Counts Append counts to nav-tree labels, e.g. Metals (42). On Show Unscanned Folders Keep folders you excluded with Scan on This Machine (nav tree, right-click) visible as dimmed (not scanned) entries. Saved per machine. On Prefer 16-bit Textures When a set ships 8- and 16-bit versions of a map, pick 16-bit. Applies on the next library refresh. Off Name Texture Nodes After File Name texture nodes after the texture file (extension stripped) instead of the channel (basecolor, normal, …). Applies to newly imported materials. Off Viewport Drop Targets Hit Component A material dropped on geometry in the Scene Viewer goes to the part under the cursor (material slot / named part in OBJ, GeomSubset in Solaris), or the whole object when no part is found. Ctrl+drop flips this for one drop. On Debug Logging Print diagnostic detail to the Python Shell: why a library re-scanned, which thumbnails failed to load, errors that are otherwise silent. JELIB_DEBUG=1 in the environment does the same for a session that cannot reach this panel. Off Copy Diagnostics (button) Copy build, Houdini, library and environment details plus the most recent log lines to the clipboard, ready to paste into a bug report. Works with Debug Logging off, but only what was logged since the panel opened is included. —

docs.title: USD
docs.text:
How non-USD geometry (see Supported file formats) enters a Solaris/LOPs stage.

Setting Options Default USD Import Mode Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Bake .usd Auto USD Import As Reference · Sublayer Reference Use Baked Cache Reference an up-to-date baked .usd directly instead of rebuilding the Component Builder chain. On Proxy Detail (%) Polyreduce percentage for the proxy purpose when baking (1–100). Also caps the collision (simproxy) hulls. Animated $F sequences bake neither. 10 Cache to $HIP Write USD caches under $HIP/usd/… instead of next to the source asset — handy when the library folder is read-only or you'll collect with the hip later. Off Clean Up After Bake After baking, remove the Component Builder nodes and leave just the reference/sublayer. On

Import Mode in brief

Auto bakes a sidecar .usd when the source folder is writable, else falls back to SOP Create (no disk write). Component Builder builds a live chain. Bake .usd always writes <asset_dir>/usd/<name>.usd. A rigged/animated FBX has its own skeleton-aware modes — see Animation & sequences.

docs.title: Geometry Import
docs.text:
Simple Import (off by default) brings geometry in as just a file/Alembic SOP plus an OUT null — skipping the xform, attribdelete, material, matchsize, and connectivity nodes.

Split Pieces — what happens when a model is made of several named objects:

Option What you get Off One output for the whole model. SOP Network (default) One extra output per named piece inside the geo. OBJ Network A subnet holding the import plus one geometry object per piece.

Greyed out while Simple Import is on — that mode builds no chain to split.

Below it, one card per format — FBX, OBJ, ABC — each with the same four controls:

Control Options FBX OBJ ABC Scale import scale (e.g. 0.01 = cm→m) 0.01 0.01 0.01 Match Size None · Match Size · Match Size (Auto Scale) None None None Attrib Delete strip helper/detail attributes On Off Off Material SOP build the Material SOP On On On

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Setting What it does On-Demand Caching on This Machine Per-machine master switch: pull remote-backed libraries into a local cache as you use them. Leave off on a machine that already has the assets locally. See Remote & cloud libraries. Trust Cloud Library Cache Without Verifying Skip re-checking cloud-synced libraries (Dropbox / OneDrive / iCloud / Synology Drive) for changes on every reload — much faster on a slow mount, but a plain Reload won't notice new or removed files. Off by default; saved per machine. See Remote & cloud libraries. Prefetch Selected Cloud / NAS Assets While browsing, download the selected asset from its remote source in the background so dropping it is instant. On-demand libraries only; saved per machine. Thumbnail Cache Folder for the pre-scaled thumbnail cache. Defaults to $JE_ASSET_BROWSER_CACHE (set in the package JSON). Auto-generate on Save Render a geometry thumbnail automatically when a 3D asset is saved via Save Asset…. Right-click → Generate Thumbnail always works regardless.

Two buttons: Cache Thumbnails pre-scales every preview into the cache; Clear Cache deletes pre-scaled thumbnails and generated geometry, material, HDRI, and texture previews. For the full workflow — and the difference between generating and caching — see Make thumbnails.

docs.title: Thumbnail Appearance
docs.text:
Controls how generated thumbnails look — see Make thumbnails.

Setting Options / effect Default Caption Alignment Center · Left · Right Center Use Simple Sphere Render on a plain sphere instead of the shaderball — better for tiling materials. Off Use HDRI Light the preview with an HDRI instead of the default studio lights. Off HDRI Path Custom HDRI file (enabled when Use HDRI is on). Leave empty for the HDA default. HDA default

docs.title: Remote & cloud libraries
docs.text: Your libraries don't have to live on the local disk. JElib works with libraries on cloud storage (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, iCloud, Synology Drive) and on a NAS / remote source — including files that are online-only (no local copy yet). It scans them safely and pulls files down only when you actually use them.

docs.title: Two flavours
docs.text:
• Cloud-sync folders (Dropbox / Drive / OneDrive / iCloud / Synology Drive) — files may be online-only placeholders. JElib browses them and pulls on load. Cloud is pull-only — it can fetch a placeholder but can't evict it back.
  • NAS / remote source with on-demand caching — a master copy lives on the remote; a local cache mirrors it as you use assets. This one you can pull and push back to online-only.

docs.title: Safe scanning
docs.text: JElib scans cloud and NAS libraries from their file listing only — reading small metadata and existing preview images, never the heavy textures/geo/HDRIs. So adding a big cloud library won't mass-download it. Heavy files stay online-only until you load them.

docs.title: Availability at a glance
docs.text:
Every asset shows where it lives:

Where you see it Meaning Grid tile — ✓ dot Synced locally, ready Grid tile — ☁ dot Remote-only but reachable, hydrates on load Grid tile — ! dot Remote unreachable — can't load until reconnected Preview panel ● Local cache: Synced / ● Local cache: Online-only — and while a prefetch runs, a live Prefetching… X / Y MB that turns Synced when done. With prefetch off it reads Online-only · Prefetch off. Libraries tab, Status Cloud = folder present but empty (still syncing/paused)

Hover the ☁ dot for a plain-language reason (e.g. Online-only — files download on first load).

docs.title: Loading pulls it down
docs.text:
Import an online-only asset and JElib downloads it first, then wires it up:

  • Cloud placeholders hydrate before the import with a cancelable Downloading… X / Y MB dialog. If the source is offline it stops cleanly and loads nothing, rather than half-importing.
  • NAS / on-demand libraries download in the background — keep browsing while the files pull; the import fires the moment they land. Load more assets and they queue behind it. The preview panel's cache line tracks progress (Caching Asset… X / Y MB · 1 queued · Esc cancels); Esc cancels the download and every queued import, and switching to a different scene cancels them too — an import never lands in a scene you didn't load it into. Files that finished downloading stay cached either way.

Prefetch while you browse

Turn on Prefetch Selected Cloud / NAS Assets (Preferences → Caching) and JElib starts pulling the selected asset in the background as you browse, so dropping it is instant. The preview panel's cache line counts it down live (Prefetching… X / Y MB → Synced).

docs.title: Make available offline / online-only
docs.text:
Right-click assets in the grid (or a library in the nav tree):

  • Make Available Offline — pull the selected assets local ahead of time.
  • Make Online-only — (NAS libraries only) delete the local copies to reclaim space. JElib only removes files it has verified still exist on the remote — it never deletes your only copy.

To manage a whole library at once, use Measure / Evict Library… in the Libraries tab inspector — same safety rules, applied library-wide.

docs.title: Setting up an on-demand (NAS) library
docs.text:
Two paths are involved, and it matters which is which:

  • Remote Source Root — where the master files live (the NAS/remote path). JElib only ever reads from here.
  • Path (the library's normal path) — the local cache on your machine's disk. Files copied here as you use assets; imported nodes always reference this path, never the NAS.

The two must mirror the same folder structure — JElib maps a file between them by its relative path. For example:

Remote Source Root:  //NAS/assets/LookdevArchive
Path (local cache):  D:/AssetCache/LookdevArchive

In the Libraries tab inspector:

  1. Tick Enable On-Demand Caching.
  2. Set Remote Source Root to the NAS path. The library's Path stays your local cache folder (it can start empty — it fills as you load assets).

On-demand caching is a per-machine opt-in (your package JSON sets JELIB_ONDEMAND_CACHE), so the same synced config can cache on one machine and read direct on another.

Machines without the remote variable just work

If a library's Remote Source Root starts with a variable that isn't set on the current machine (say $STUDIO_NAS on a laptop that has everything local), JElib simply reads the library from its local folder — live, with no warnings. The only trace is a note on the count in the Libraries tab. Scans on such a machine aren't cached, so set the variable (or clear the Remote Source Root) if it's meant to be permanent.

docs.title: One config, many machines
docs.text:
JElib stores library paths relative to a per-machine base variable, $JELIB_ASSETS, so a single synced config resolves everywhere:

  • Each machine points $JELIB_ASSETS at wherever its copy of the assets lives (set on first run, or edit it in the package JSON).
  • Library paths are written $JELIB_ASSETS/<name> — use Use Relative Path in the Libraries inspector to convert an absolute path to the portable form.
  • Sync user_libraries.json and favorites.json between machines; every library resolves against each machine's $JELIB_ASSETS.

The first-run setup detects cloud providers (Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive, iCloud Drive, Synology Drive) and offers them as one-click picks. For a NAS mirror, point the optional $JELIB_ASSETS_REMOTE at the remote and JElib derives each library's remote from its local path — no per-library setup.

Bringing up a second machine, step by step:

  1. Install JElib as usual (see Installation).
  2. On first run, pick (or edit in the package JSON) where this machine's assets live — that becomes its $JELIB_ASSETS.
  3. Copy or sync user_libraries.json and favorites.json from the first machine.
  4. If this machine caches from a NAS: set $JELIB_ASSETS_REMOTE to the NAS base and JELIB_ONDEMAND_CACHE = 1 in the package JSON. A machine that has everything locally just leaves caching off — same config, no changes.
  5. Open the browser — libraries resolve against this machine's $JELIB_ASSETS; the shared scan cache means no full first-scan of a big synced library.

Enable per machine

Enabled on This Machine (Libraries inspector, or Disable on This Machine in the nav tree) turns a library on or off for this computer only — your synced library list and favorites are untouched.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• A plain Reload click always fully re-checks every NAS library by default. This is deliberately the safe, accurate choice — it reflects whatever's actually on the NAS right now, even though a full re-check is exactly as slow as a NAS-backed library is to browse in the first place. New or removed files always show up after a Reload, with nothing to configure.
  • If a library is basically frozen and you'd rather trust the last scan for speed, right-click it in the nav tree → Trust Cache on Reload. Once on, a plain Reload click for that library skips the network check entirely and just shows what was last saved — fast, but it won't notice anything added, changed, or removed on the NAS until you force a real check: Shift- or Ctrl-click Reload (forces every library, ignoring this setting), or right-click the library → Reload This Library (forces just that one — this option also ignores Trust Cache on Reload, it's always a real check). Turn Trust Cache on Reload back off any time to go back to the always-accurate default. Off by default on purpose, same reasoning as Trust Cloud Library Cache below — a stale cache should never be served silently unless you've explicitly asked for that trade-off.
  • If you never touch part of a vendor library on this machine (a Greyscalegorilla hdris folder on a laptop, say), right-click that folder in the nav tree and uncheck Scan on This Machine — a whole type folder or a single vendor collection. That subtree is never walked, cached, or thumbnailed here again; it stays in the tree as a dimmed (not scanned) entry so you can turn it back on from the same place. Saved per machine — your other machines keep scanning it.
  • Cloud-sync libraries (Dropbox/Drive/OneDrive/iCloud/Synology Drive) are fully re-checked on every reload by default — same as a plain local library, just slower the bigger/more-remote the library is. If that's too slow and you'd rather trust the cache instead, turn on Preferences → Caching → Trust Cloud Library Cache Without Verifying — once on, these libraries behave exactly like the NAS case above: a plain Reload click won't notice new/removed files, only Shift/Ctrl-click Reload or a per-library force-reload will. Off by default on purpose — an already-existing but wrong/outdated cache can otherwise get served with nothing telling you it's stale.
  • Only the asset's primary files are pulled. A USD asset that references other files internally, or a saved node-tree material with external textures, pulls its main file — the rest resolve from the remote or may be missing locally. After a load, the cache status line reports anything that stayed remote.
  • Online-only $F image sequences can't be pulled yet — they keep the cloud indicator.
  • Pulled files accumulate — there's no automatic local eviction (use Make Online-only on NAS libraries to reclaim space).

docs.title: Renderers
docs.text: When you import a PBR asset, JElib builds a complete, wired material for your active renderer — every map connected to the right input, in the right color space, ready to render. No manual shader work.

docs.title: The three renderers
docs.text:
JElib supports Redshift, Octane, and Karma, in both the OBJ//mat and LOP/Solaris contexts. Pick your engine with the toolbar renderer selector — your choice is remembered across sessions.

In Solaris, JElib builds inside a materiallibrary and wires the assignment for you; in OBJ it builds a native material container and assigns it via a Material SOP.

If a renderer isn't installed

If the chosen renderer's plugin isn't loaded, JElib skips the material and still loads the geometry — no broken nodes. Switch the selector to a renderer you have installed and re-import to get the shader.

docs.title: The material it builds
docs.text:
By default JElib builds each renderer's standard surface. Switch Preferences → Import → Material Type to Open PBR for the OpenPBR surface instead:

Renderer Standard Open PBR Redshift redshift::StandardMaterial redshift::OpenPBRMaterial Octane Standard Surface Open PBR Surface Karma mtlxstandard_surface mtlxopen_pbr_surface

docs.title: What gets wired
docs.text:
For a full PBR set, JElib connects the maps it finds:

  • Base color, roughness, metalness, specular, opacity, emission
  • Normal / bump / height (see below)
  • Sheen, coat, anisotropy, translucency / SSS when present — a translucency map even switches on subsurface automatically

Color space is handled for you: color maps as sRGB, data maps (roughness, metal, normal, height) as raw. Packed maps (ORM-style occlusion/roughness/translucency) are split to the right inputs, and a glossiness map is inverted into roughness when no roughness map exists.

AO maps aren't connected

Ambient-occlusion maps are not wired — the standard surfaces have no AO input. Composite AO into your base color beforehand if you need it.

docs.title: Normal, bump & displacement
docs.text:
Preferences → Import → Bump Map Mode decides how surface detail is wired:

  • Normal Map (default) — use the normal map; fall back to a bump/height map only when there's no normal map.
  • Bump Map — prefer a dedicated bump map over the normal map.
  • Displacement — route the height map through the renderer's displacement output instead of bump.

Each renderer uses its native nodes for this (Redshift BumpMap/Displacement, Karma mtlxnormalmap/mtlxdisplacement, Octane's normal/bump/displacement slots), and respects a normal-strength value if the set ships one.

docs.title: UV or triplanar
docs.text:
Preferences → Import → Default Projection:

  • UV — standard UV sampling, with shared Scale / Offset / Rotate controls on the material.
  • Triplanar — world-space projection, no UV unwrap needed. A triplanar node is inserted per texture; the Scale/Offset/Rotate controls don't apply.

You can also override projection per import in the preview panel.

docs.title: Where the material lives & how it's assigned
docs.text:
Preferences → Import → Material Network controls where the material is built. The default, Current Network, follows the viewer — it builds a per-asset matnet in whatever network you're looking at (or directly inside a matnet/vopnet you're already in), falling back to /mat in a non-material context. The fixed overrides are a per-asset matnet inside the geo network (SOP Context), a shared /mat (Global), or a shared /obj/matnet (OBJ Context).

In OBJ/SOP, a Material SOP assigns the material by shop_materialpath (or by name attribute — see Material Assignment). In Solaris, a materiallibrary → assignmaterial chain does it. Either way JElib also adds viewport-preview textures so the asset shows shaded before you render.

docs.title: Save to the browser
docs.text: The browser goes both ways: build a shader or a node setup in Houdini, then save it back into a library so you can reuse it anywhere. Saved setups rebuild exactly as you left them — parameters, connections, ramps, and all.

docs.title: What you can save
docs.text:
Any network you can select — a Redshift / Octane / Karma material builder, a subnet, a whole material network, or a group of loose nodes. JElib detects the renderer automatically, so there's nothing to tag.

  • Select container nodes (each holding a network) and each is saved as its own asset.
  • Select loose nodes (or a mix) and they're saved together as one asset — they just have to share the same parent network.
  • Select only ramp nodes or Color SOPs and they're saved as a color palette (.ase) rather than a node asset — see Color palettes.

docs.title: Save it
docs.text:
You need two things first: nodes selected in the network editor, and a destination folder selected in the browser's nav tree (it must be one of your own writable libraries — vendor libraries can't be written to).

Then, either:

  • Right-click the node(s) in the network editor → Save Asset [JE], or
  • Drag the selected nodes onto a folder in the browser's nav tree, or onto the grid.

JElib asks for a name and saves. The asset appears in the grid under Node Trees, badged with its renderer (REDSHIFT, OCTANE, KARMA, or NODE).

Overwriting an existing asset

Saving under a name that already exists asks first — Overwrite or Cancel. While iterating on the same setup, tick Don't ask again for this asset this session and JElib stops prompting for that asset until you reload the panel. Saving under a new name never prompts.

docs.title: Reuse it
docs.text: Import a saved setup like any other asset — drag it in, double-click, or Load into Scene. See Import into your scene. JElib rebuilds the network for its renderer.

docs.title: Thumbnails for saved assets
docs.text: With Auto-generate on Save on (Preferences → Caching), JElib renders a thumbnail for each saved 3D asset automatically. Either way you can right-click the asset → Generate Thumbnail at any time — see Make thumbnails.

docs.title: Working in Solaris (USD)
docs.text: JElib works natively in Solaris. Drop an asset into a LOP network / stage and it builds USD — references, materials, and instancing all native to the stage — instead of the SOP-based setup you'd get in OBJ.

docs.title: It follows your context
docs.text:
Dropping into a Solaris network builds USD automatically — JElib reads the network editor you dropped into, so a multi-asset drop keeps landing in the same stage. Dropping into OBJ builds the classic geo network instead.

Import Into Active Network

The stage is used when Import Into Active Network (Preferences → Import → Advanced) is on. Turn it off to always create a fresh top-level container regardless of where you drop.

docs.title: Bringing non-USD geometry into the stage
docs.text:
Models that aren't already USD (see Supported file formats) can enter the stage several ways. Set the default in Preferences → USD → USD Import Mode; override per import in the preview panel's LOP Import:

Mode What lands in the stage Writes to disk? Auto (default) Bakes a .usd sidecar and references it if the asset folder is writable; otherwise falls back to SOP Create Only if writable SOP Create A sopcreate LOP wrapping the import chain No Component Builder A live, editable componentgeometry → componentoutput chain No Bake .usd Always writes <asset>/usd/<name>.usd and references it Yes Use Cached USD References an existing baked .usd as-is — never rebuilds No

The preview panel labels these USD Auto Import · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD · Use Cached USD; a rigged/animated FBX swaps the last two build modes for USD Skel and Bake USD — see Animation & sequences.

Only the baking modes (Bake, and Auto when it can write) produce a reusable .usd on disk — SOP Create and Component Builder keep everything live in the scene, which is heavier and can't be reused across drops.

docs.title: Reference or sublayer
docs.text:
Preferences → USD → USD Import As controls how the asset composes into the stage:

  • Reference (default) — a reference LOP brings the asset in under its own prim, /<asset_name>. The standard way to bring in a contained asset.
  • Sublayer — a sublayer LOP merges the file's own layer structure into the stage as-is.

docs.title: Native USD assets
docs.text: A .usd / .usdc / .usda / .usdz asset is referenced directly — no baking, no SOP import — following your Reference/Sublayer choice. Multi-variant USD plants come in as a single reference with one prim per variant.

docs.title: Baking & reusing caches
docs.text:
When a mode bakes, JElib writes to <asset>/usd/<name>/… next to the source by default. Two preferences change and reuse that:

  • Cache to $HIP — write caches under $HIP/usd/… instead, handy when the asset folder is read-only or you'll collect everything with the hip later. (Save your scene first — an unsaved hip falls back to the asset folder with a warning.)
  • Use Baked Cache — when an up-to-date .usd cache already exists, reference it directly instead of rebuilding the Component Builder chain. Much lighter for production scenes.
  • Clean Up After Bake — after baking, remove the Component Builder nodes and leave just the reference. Re-baking then needs a fresh import.
  • Proxy Detail (%) — how much the Component Builder reduces the proxy representation when baking. Doesn't apply to a $F sequence bake — those author no proxy.

Animated sources bake animated

A $F sequence bakes as a time-sampled USD over its own frame range, not a frozen first frame, and only re-bakes when its frames change — with no proxy or collision representation (static assets only). A rigged FBX bakes as a real UsdSkel component, with its own proxy. Either can Loop for the whole scene range. See Animation & sequences.

docs.title: Materials in the stage
docs.text:
JElib builds a materiallibrary and wires a material assignment onto the imported prims for you — per renderer, the shader lives in that library (rs_usd_material_builder for Redshift, octane_solaris_material_builder for Octane, an mtlx subnet for Karma). See Renderers & materials for what gets wired.

Viewport preview

Redshift and Octane materials also get a UsdPreviewSurface so they shade in the GL/Storm viewport. Karma's MaterialX shaders preview natively, so they don't get one — a non-Karma Storm viewport may show a Karma material flat.

docs.title: Houdini's native galleries
docs.text:
JElib also registers as a Solaris asset gallery data source, so your libraries appear inside Houdini's own USD tools:

  • Layout Asset Gallery / Stage Manager / Paint Instances — the shared layout gallery defaults to JElib Library on startup and lists your model libraries in their folder hierarchy (vendor libraries group by pack or collection). Rigged/ animated FBX and $F frame sequences appear here alongside static models; VDB and .rs proxy sequences don't, since they import through the volume/proxy LOPs rather than the gallery's model bake.
  • Material Catalog / Material Linker — pick JElib Library from the catalog's source menu to list your materials there.

You can also drag directly from the JElib grid into Stage Manager, Paint Instances or the Material Linker — the drag carries Houdini's own asset payload, so the native tools accept it like one of their items.

Materials dropped this way bake to a small standalone .usd next to the asset (or under $HIP with Cache to $HIP) that references the textures in place — one file per renderer, built with the active renderer's shader network and the panel's Material Type. Delete USD Cache in the preview panel removes them. Paths follow Force Absolute File Paths, so gallery references stay portable.

docs.title: Kits & asset packs
docs.text:
A multi-model FBX kit — a full city kit, a props pack — bakes as a USD assembly holding a component per model. What that buys you:

  • A gallery card per model. The Asset Catalog fans the kit out into one card per building; the whole-kit card still drops the city in its authored layout.
  • Light references. Each model writes a small USD of its own beside the pack, so referencing one building from Stage Manager never opens the whole city.
  • Scattering picks models. Create Instances on a kit mixes the kit's models as prototypes (both instance methods), and a Choose models toggle in the inspector opens a picker for which pieces scatter — leave the dumpsters out.
  • Per-model viewport proxies. Every model carries proxy geometry: dense pieces decimated, small pieces passed through, very heavy pieces (500k+ faces) a bounding box — so a scattered city stays responsive in the viewport.

Kit detection is automatic (all meshes named into groups, 8 or more groups), and the cards get their pictures from the viewport moments after the bake lands.

docs.title: Instancing in the stage
docs.text:
With Create Instances on, a Solaris import builds a native USD PointInstancer rather than the SOP copy-to-points setup used in OBJ. The same distribution and wind controls apply.

Which LOP it lands as depends on the instance method picked in the preview panel, and on your Houdini version:

Method H20.5 / H21 H22 Copy to Points (default) the Instancer LOP the same node, renamed Copy to Points — matching its SOP counterpart Scatter Instances (H22) not available the Scatter Instances LOP, which scatters onto a surface and authors the PointInstancer in one node

Same node, new name

H22 renamed the Instancer LOP to Copy to Points; scenes and scripts using the old instancer type still resolve to it. Scatter Instances is a separate, H22-only node — the panel greys the option out on older builds.

Per-instance time offset in the stage

An animated asset with Create Instances on gets a Cache LOP + Retime Instances with bucketed per-instance offsets, so scattered copies play the animation at their own phase on a native USD PointInstancer — not lockstep. The retime wrangle exposes Bucket Count (how many distinct offsets — each one costs a prototype, so it's the cost dial) and Seed; everything else is automatic. See Per-instance time offset.

Several animated assets can share one crowd. Multi-select two or more Create-Instances models (at least one animated) and drop them together: they merge into one instancer — one scatter mixing every asset as prototypes, each copy offset within its own asset's clip length. Anything that can't safely join — a kit, two assets claiming the same stage prim, an animated asset that hasn't baked yet — automatically keeps its own separate chain, and the footer says why.

.abc sequences stay excluded from Create Instances everywhere — every offset copy would need its own archive open, which is unusably slow. Bake to .bgeo.sc and instance that instead.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Renderer not installed? The USD geometry still loads — the material is just skipped, so you get untextured geo. Switch to an installed renderer and re-import.
  • Read-only asset folder? Auto quietly falls back to SOP Create (no cache). Use Bake .usd + Cache to $HIP to force a reusable cache elsewhere.
  • Proxy Detail, Component Builder, and material building don't apply to native USD files — those are referenced exactly as authored.

docs.title: Make thumbnails
